name: Eternalism
statement: Past, present, and future all equally exist; the flow of time is a perspective, not a fact.
statementAccent: Past, present, and future all equally exist
meaning: Eternalism is the view in the metaphysics of time that all times, past, present, and future, are equally real and equally exist. Past events, such as dinosaurs, and future events exist just as much as present ones; they are simply located at different times, much as distant places exist though they are not here. On this picture the universe is a four-dimensional block, a static spacetime manifold in which all events at all times are equally real, often called the block universe. The present, or now, is not metaphysically privileged; it is indexical, like here or I, picking out merely the time of an utterance, so that every time is present relative to itself, and there is no objective, moving present and no objective passage or flow of time, the sense of flow being at best perspectival or mind-dependent. Eternalism is typically associated with the B-theory of time, the tenseless theory that describes time through the earlier-than and later-than relations of McTaggart's B-series, in contrast to the tensed A-theory and to presentism. It is often argued to be supported by special relativity, since the relativity of simultaneity implies there is no unique, observer-independent present, a line pressed in the Rietdijk-Putnam argument by Wim Rietdijk in 1966 and Hilary Putnam in 1967, drawing on Minkowski spacetime. Einstein himself, consoling the family of his friend Besso in 1955, remarked in a much-quoted letter that the distinction between past, present, and future is a stubbornly persistent illusion.
mechanism: Eternalism treats time as another dimension along which reality is spread out, so that existence is not confined to a moving present. Just as things exist at places other than here, on eternalism things exist at times other than now; a dinosaur exists, tenselessly, at its own time, and a future outpost exists at its time, and all these times are equally part of the one four-dimensional block. Because no time is metaphysically singled out, the word now works indexically, referring to whichever time the speaker occupies, exactly as here refers to the speaker's place; every moment is now from its own standpoint, and none is objectively The Present. This is why eternalism denies an objective flow of time: there is no privileged present that moves, and the vivid impression of passage must be explained as an artifact of how conscious beings are embedded in the block rather than as a feature of time itself, a stance requiring an illusionist or error-theoretic treatment of our experience. Eternalism pairs naturally with the tenseless B-theory, which analyzes temporal facts using the fixed earlier-than and later-than relations rather than the shifting past, present, and future of the A-series. The main scientific motivation comes from special relativity: since which events count as simultaneous with a given event depends on the reference frame, there is no frame-independent global present, and the Rietdijk-Putnam argument concludes that all events are equally real and determinate, a four-dimensionalist result. Eternalism as an ontological thesis, that all times exist, is related to but distinct from the B-theory, which concerns the analysis of tense.

examples.text: The universe is a four-dimensional block in which all events at all times are equally real, like places on a map.
The present is not privileged but indexical, like here; every time is present relative to itself.
Special relativity gives no frame-independent present, which the Rietdijk-Putnam argument takes to support eternalism.

whyItMatters: Eternalism is one of the two dominant positions in the metaphysics of time and the view most closely aligned with modern physics. Its importance lies in offering a coherent alternative to the common-sense picture of a flowing present, holding instead that reality is a four-dimensional whole in which all times are equally real, an idea that reshapes how we think about existence, change, and our own place in time. The block universe is often taken to be the natural metaphysics of relativistic spacetime, since the relativity of simultaneity in special relativity undercuts the objective, global present that presentism and the A-theory require, making eternalism a central case study in how metaphysics should respond to science, as the Rietdijk-Putnam argument and Einstein's own remark about the illusion of past, present, and future illustrate. The debate between eternalism and presentism has structured the philosophy of time and sharpened our understanding of tense, passage, and the reality of the present, drawing on McTaggart's distinction between the A-series and the B-series. Eternalism also raises profound questions about the experience of time's flow, about change, and about freedom and the openness of the future.

working.text: hold that all times, past, present, and future, are equally real, like a four-dimensional block.
deny a privileged moving present, letting now pick out merely the speaker's time.
regard the felt flow of time as perspectival or illusory rather than an objective feature of the block.

limits: Eternalism faces objections centered on our experience of time and on the interpretation of physics. The most pressing is the appearance of temporal passage: it seems undeniable that time flows, that the present is special and advances, and that the future is open, yet eternalism must treat this pervasive experience as an illusion or as merely perspectival, which requires a demanding illusionist or error-theoretic account of why time seems to pass if it does not. Relatedly, eternalism must explain change without a moving present, typically by analyzing it as variation across the tenseless block, which some find unsatisfying. Worries about fatalism arise, since if future events are already real it can seem that the future is fixed and human freedom illusory, though eternalists deny that ontological reality entails determinism. The support from special relativity, while influential, is contested, since some argue metaphysics need not simply read its ontology off current physics. Some details reward care: eternalism as an ontology is distinct from the B-theory of tense, the Rietdijk-Putnam dates are 1966 and 1967, and the Einstein letter of 1955 exists in varying translations, so its exact wording should be handled cautiously.
misreadings: Eternalism does not deny that events are ordered in time or that there are earlier and later moments; it denies only that one moment is objectively and uniquely present. It is not the claim that nothing changes, since change is analyzed as variation across times within the block. And the reality of the future does not by itself entail fatalism or determinism, which are separate theses, so treating eternalism as erasing temporal order, as denying change, or as implying that the future is fated, misreads the view.
origin: The view in the metaphysics of time that all times are equally real, the four-dimensional block universe, associated with the tenseless B-theory and argued to be supported by special relativity, contrasted with presentism and the A-theory.
